extracted.intended_audience: small business owners, small-business representatives, and advocates who want to participate in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing and submitting effective public comment letters and participating in the federal notice-and-comment rulemaking process, with emphasis on small business considerations under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed cost information and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies value comments that provide detailed cost information and alternative ways of achieving a statutory goal. The length of the letter is not the most important factor; providing data and detail is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give actual cost numbers or as specific estimates as possible; quantify impacts on your business; propose alternative, flexible ways to accomplish the rule’s objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include your full name and address
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 1. Your full name and address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear contact information so the agency can associate the comment with a real affected party and follow up if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly reference the rule name
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 2. Correct reference to the name of the rule you are commenting on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the exact rule title, docket number, and any identifying information from the NPRM to ensure your comment is associated with the correct rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain what's at stake for you/business
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 3. An explanation of what is at stake for you and your business in this rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the specific interests, business lines, customers, or operations that would be affected by the rule to demonstrate standing and concrete impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific details and examples of impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 4. Details and examples of how the rule will affect your business, customers, production, policy, and products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples, operational descriptions, and data showing how compliance costs, timelines, or market effects would change; explain real-world implementation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make clear requests or recommendations to improve the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 5. Clear requests or recommendations to improve the rule, for instance: to delay it for a certain number of days to provide more time to comply; to revise a particular part of it; to exclude a part of the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State specific regulatory text changes, requested carve-outs, compliance timelines, or alternative regulatory approaches; avoid vague objections—offer actionable fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a summary of your comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 6. A summary of your comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin or end with a concise summary that highlights the main points and requested outcomes to make it easier for agency reviewers to grasp the core message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a polite closing/word of thanks
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comment letters include: 7. A word of thanks to the agency for considering the rule’s small business impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A brief courteous closing helps maintain professional tone and constructive engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note the comment deadline and file timely
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not forget. Be sure to note the comment deadline. They are different for each rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the deadline in the NPRM, plan submission logistics, and submit before the close of the comment period (e.g., via regulations.gov) to ensure your input is part of the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to file comments (regulations.gov / Federal Register)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most comment letters are filed online at https://regulations.gov. They can also be mailed, faxed, or emailed. The address is listed in the proposed rule in the Federal Register, available at www.federalregister.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the submission instructions in the NPRM; include docket number and rule reference; keep proof of submission when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment period expectations (typical length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comment period (frequently 60 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to prepare substantive comments within the stated comment period; if more time is needed, request extensions or note timing in outreach to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA principle: consider small entity impacts and provide flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Flexibility Act established the principle that government agencies must consider the effects of their rules on small entities, and where possible, they must provide flexibility to reduce negative impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commenting, highlight small-entity impacts and propose flexible/regulatory alternatives that achieve statutory goals with lower burdens on small businesses; Advocacy monitors agency compliance with this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) or certification at proposal stage
rubrics_metrics.description: RFA requirement: Agency must either: a. Certify rule will not have major small business impact or b. Publish an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency certifies no significant impact, commenters may challenge that certification by providing data showing significant small-entity impacts and arguing an IRFA is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) requirement at final rule stage
rubrics_metrics.description: RFA requirement: If an initial regulatory flexibility analysis was required, final rule must include a final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FRFA must address comments, explain the agency’s consideration of small entity impacts and alternatives, and respond to Advocacy’s and public comments on small business impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: SBREFA panel requirement for CFPB, EPA, and OSHA
rubrics_metrics.description: A special requirement applies to three agencies: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Environmental Protection Agency, and Occupational Safety and Health Administration. When one of them begins considering a new regulation that will have a significant impact on small entities, it must convene a small business review panel (SBREFA panel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SBREFA panels consider approaches to regulation and solicit small business input early; small businesses should engage in these panels or through representatives to influence rule design.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review under Executive Order 12866 for 'significant' rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) reviews and coordinates rules written by executive branch agencies that will cost the economy $100 million or more. While a proposed rule is under review, any affected entity can ask for a meeting to provide information on how the rule might affect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize OIRA review as an additional opportunity for advocacy (request E.O. 12866 meetings); note that independent agencies are not subject to OIRA review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements of the final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is lengthy. In addition to stating all the requirements of the rule in detail, it contains the purpose and justifications of the rule, summaries of the comments received, and the effective date or dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted become part of the record summarized in the final rule; cite evidence and arguments you want the agency to address in that summary and in any required FRFA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for how public comments affect agency decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must base its reasoning and conclusions on the rulemaking record, consisting of the comments, scientific data, expert opinions, and facts accumulated during the pre-rule and proposed rule stages. It must also consider whether alternate solutions would be more effective or cost less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence-based, factual, and expert-backed comments; pose substantive critiques or offer alternative solutions to influence agency reasoning; purely numerical counts of support/opposition do not determine outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes depending on comment record (terminate, revise, supplemental NPRM, or proceed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rulemaking record contains persuasive new data or policy arguments, or poses difficult questions or criticisms, the agency may decide to terminate the rulemaking. Or, the agency may decide to continue the rulemaking but change aspects of the rule. If the changes are major, the agency may publish a supplemental proposed rule. If the changes are minor, or a logical outgrowth of the issues and solutions discussed in the proposed rules, the agency may proceed with a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help agencies identify whether submitted evidence warrants major vs. minor changes by clearly explaining implications and recommended textual changes; indicate if a supplemental NPRM is appropriate when your suggested changes are not a straightforward refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the notice-and-comment process
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain cases, agencies issue rules without notice and comment. Reasons for this may include military or foreign affairs functions, internal agency procedures, contracts, interpretive rules, guidance, or for good cause, such as a national emergency. In such cases agencies may issue interim final rules or direct final rules, to which the RFA does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a rule is exempt from notice-and-comment; if exempt, RFA-related small business procedures normally will not apply—advocacy opportunities may be different or limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 610 Ten-Year Review requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 610 of the RFA requires agencies to review rules that have or will have a significant small entity impact within 10 years of their promulgation to determine whether they should be continued as is, amended, or rescinded to minimize their impact on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small businesses can provide input during these periodic 10-year reviews to argue for amendment or rescission of burdensome rules; note the review obligation when planning regulatory reform outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Orders on regulatory reform (EO13771 and EO13777)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 13771 requires that any new regulation be balanced by removing at least two other regulations, and that costs of new regulations be offset by eliminating costs of existing ones. Executive Order 13777 created a framework for reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regulatory reform initiatives and roundtables to highlight especially burdensome rules and propose deregulatory replacements or offsets consistent with these executive orders.
